messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

DeAndre was forty-six when he finally sat in the intake chair, but the weight that brought him there had settled in over three years, beginning on a humid July night outside a community center where a routine delivery run had curdled into a traumatic police stop. The cruiser’s headlights had blinded him before the loudspeaker crackled with abrupt, overlapping commands. He remembers the sudden jolt of his car door being wrenched open, the rough grip on his shoulders, the hard press of a knee against his spine as he was forced face-down onto the cracked pavement, and the metallic taste of panic flooding his mouth while officers shouted about a nonexistent warrant. That specific collision of blinding lights, shouted directives, and the sudden, crushing weight against his body created a precise trigger map: any flash of blue or white strobe light, any voice that rose in pitch or volume, any sensation of being boxed in or physically restrained would instantly activate the same neural alarm that had fired that night. Within weeks, DeAndre’s body refused to stand down. He found himself permanently scanning the periphery of the district’s curriculum design center, his eyes tracking the heavy footsteps of facilities workers and his shoulders braced whenever anyone approached his desk from behind. The open-plan workspace, originally meant to foster collaboration, became a minefield of sudden movement; a dropped binder or a conference door slamming shut made his entire torso seize, his breath catching as a heavy, electric heat radiated through his chest. He had come to believe that remaining alert was the only way to stay safe, so he stopped taking the main elevator, opting instead for the narrow service lift to avoid the lobby’s unpredictable bursts of traffic, and he began positioning his chair facing the door, knees locked under the desk. Alongside that constant state of readiness, the memory of the stop began to surface in fragments that refused to cooperate with his attempts to process them. When the recall finally broke through, usually during the quiet stretch after his children went to sleep, DeAndre would feel so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to push his chair back and step out of his office, leaving his lesson plans half-finished on the desk. He couldn’t seem to put the frightening event into words for his wife or the therapist, no matter how carefully he tried to arrange the details; the moment he opened his mouth, the sequence dissolved into static. More often, the memory arrived as emotion without image: a sudden, formless wave of cold dread that would wash over him without any clear picture, just a crushing physical weight in his gut that made his hands tremble and his throat tighten, leaving him grasping for an explanation he could not name. The two states fed directly into each other, and it was the threat symptoms that reliably pulled him into the memory. Every time his body jumped at a loud noise or his eyes caught a flicker of blue light down the corridor, the sudden physical spike of alertness acted as a key, unlocking the overwhelming, wordless recall that had been lying dormant. That jumpy, watchful tension didn’t just sit beside the fear; it directly led to the memory flood. The more he stayed on guard, the more his nervous system interpreted ordinary office sounds as danger, and each time that started his heart hammering, it funneled him straight back into the emotion without image, the sudden overwhelm that forced him to stop working and retreat. He stopped attending the weekly planning meetings because the enclosed glass room and the sudden ring of his phone triggered the same physical reactivity, which in turn dragged him into the memory, leaving him stranded between a present he couldn’t trust and a past he couldn’t articulate. Over the months, these habits quietly dismantled his routine. He began leaving the building thirty minutes early to avoid the evening shift change that always brought heavy footsteps through the parking lot, and his wife noticed how he flinched when she reached for him in the dark, sleeping on the far edge of the mattress to keep his escape route clear. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single collapse, but a quiet realization that he was living in a permanent state of defense, terrified that he would miss his daughter’s graduation because his own body would betray him in the crowd. He hopes to find a way to let his shoulders drop, even if only for an hour at a time, though he fears that stepping into the therapy room might mean opening a door he can never close again.
